take.head: Browns edge the Steelers in a field-goal game
take.lean:
Deshaun Watson throws into a Steelers secondary without Joey Porter Jr., and Jalen Ramsey (wrist) and Brandin Echols (concussion) are both questionable. Watson has been an above-average passer through three weeks. Aaron Rodgers has been one of the worst passers in the league. That gap matters more than any name on the field.

Cleveland's problem is up front. Elgton Jenkins and Teven Jenkins are both out, so two rookies start on the line against a Pittsburgh rush that sacks the quarterback on 8.6 percent of pass plays. Watson will take hits and some drives will die. He has an answer, though: he took 36.7 percent of Cleveland's carries last week and has beaten his projection three weeks running. His running holds up even against a defense that allows the fifth-fewest points to quarterbacks.

He has to keep the ball, because the Browns' running backs are no help. Cleveland's run game is the league's worst. Quinshon Judkins gets most of the carries and has still fallen short of his projection every week. He was limited at practice for personal reasons, and Raheim Sanders takes passing-down snaps. Pittsburgh ranks 22nd against backs, which keeps Judkins from a disaster, but not much more.

So the passing game carries Cleveland. Denzel Boston plays nearly every snap, and with Porter out he draws the easier corners. Harold Fannin Jr. drew 30 percent of the targets last week, but Pittsburgh ranks 8th against tight ends, so he lands near his number rather than repeating that game.

Pittsburgh is priced like last year's offense, which scored 23.4 a game with Rodgers playing well. This year's version swings from a 4.0-point week to a 22.7-point week, and the 22.7 came against Cincinnati. Jaylen Warren is the engine with Rico Dowdle out. He got 73.9 percent of the carries last week, but Cleveland's defense ranks 9th against backs, so the volume pays without a breakout.

The Steelers' path is outside. Cleveland's defense ranks 26th against wide receivers, and DK Metcalf is the receiver Rodgers looks for when a drive needs a play. That gets Pittsburgh into the red zone. Finishing is the problem: the Steelers score touchdowns on a third of their trips, and the Browns do little better at 37.5 percent. Both offenses stall inside the 20 and trade field goals, and the home team with the better quarterback this season wins the last exchange.
take.vs: Disagree on the side: the market expects PIT 20.5, CLE 18. Rodgers' passing doesn't back that up, and Cleveland's home field and better quarterback win a game this tight.
take.risk: PIT's rush overwhelms CLE's two rookie linemen, Watson takes sacks and turns it over, and Warren's workload breaks a long run.

ats.edge: PIT is priced on last year's 23.4-point offense; Rodgers has been among the league's worst passers this year, Watson above average

take.vs_blind: Held: blind had CLE by 1 and a 38.5 total. The market's PIT by 2.5 leans on Pittsburgh's name and last season. Nothing in this year's numbers supports it.

notes.text: With Rico Dowdle out again, Jaylen Warren leads the Steelers backfield after a 127-yard game against the Bengals. Expect a heavy workload.
Cleveland's run game ranks among the league's worst this year, while Watson's passing has been slightly above average. Temper Judkins hopes.
PIT ruled out CB Joey Porter Jr.; Jalen Ramsey (wrist) and Brandin Echols (concussion) are questionable. Watson's receivers get a softer matchup.

players.why: His running has beaten his projection three straight weeks, and a thin PIT secondary helps his passing.
Plays nearly every snap and draws easier corners with Porter out.
The league's worst run game behind a patched line, plus limited practice; short of his projection every week.
A big target share, but PIT ranks 8th against tight ends, so no repeat of last week.
Huge carry share with Dowdle out, but CLE ranks 9th against backs.
CLE ranks 26th against wide receivers, and he's Rodgers' go-to on key downs.
A soft secondary against wideouts offsets a season of poor passing, and red-zone stalls cap him.

take.head: Colts edge it, Mariota keeps Washington close
take.lean:
Jonathan Taylor runs into a wall in London. Washington's defense ranks 2nd against running backs and has stuffed the run all season. That puts this game on Daniel Jones's arm, and Washington's pass defense is where the points are. It ranks dead last against wide receivers and 31st against tight ends.

Jones has been the worst part of the Colts' offense. He has been sacked often, his passes have gained almost nothing, and he keeps giving the ball away. Some of that is bad luck: the Colts lost 3 of 4 fumbles. He was efficient all of last year, and this is the defense where he gets back on track. Keenan Allen is out and Alec Pierce is on IR, so his throws have only two places to go. Josh Downs drew a 31.4 percent target share last week. Tyler Warren's share has gone up every week, and he plays almost every snap. Expect both to beat their projections while Taylor gets his carries and few yards.

The Colts won't pull away, though, because their own defense is just as bad. Indianapolis ranks 29th against quarterbacks and gives up more than 30 points a game. Marcus Mariota has kept Washington's passing game working without Jayden Daniels. He scored 20.4 points last week, many of them on his own runs, and those runs don't depend on who is catching passes. With Terry McLaurin and Rachaad White out, Stefon Diggs gets nearly every short throw that matters.

Washington's ground game is the weak spot. Indianapolis ranks 28th against backs, but Jacory Croskey-Merritt has done little with a lead role. Austin Ekeler now takes part of that work, which keeps both of them near their projections. Washington's points come from Mariota and Diggs moving the ball through the air.

This turns into a passing game on both sides, with two secondaries that can't stop anyone. Indianapolis wins because Jones has the better targets left. Washington stays within a field goal because the Colts' turnovers give it extra possessions.
take.vs: Higher on both teams. The implied 21 for Washington ignores an Indianapolis defense ranked 29th against QBs, and two leaky pass defenses push the total over.
take.risk: Taylor breaks through Washington's run defense and the Colts pull away on the ground, or Jones throws away more possessions.

ats.edge: The move to IND by 4.5 over-prices Daniels' absence; Mariota has kept the pass game working and Jones keeps giving the ball away.

take.vs_blind: Moved from IND by 1.5 to IND by 3. The blind already had Mariota starting, so the market's full swing overcharges Washington. Total up from 45.5: two pass defenses that leak.

notes.text: Josh Downs should get the most Colts targets. Keenan Allen (groin) is out and Alec Pierce is on IR, so he has little competition.
Jonathan Taylor has 325 total yards and 4 TDs, but Washington has stuffed the run this year. He was held to 68 yards on 23 carries in Week 3.
With McLaurin and Rachaad White out, Mariota will lean on Stefon Diggs and short throws. TE Chig Okonkwo returns from a hamstring injury.

players.why: With Allen out and Pierce on IR, he leads the targets against the defense that allows the most to WRs.
His target share has climbed every week, and Washington ranks 31st against tight ends.
Washington ranks 2nd against backs; he gets the carries but not the yards.
Indianapolis ranks 29th against QBs, and his legs gave him 20.4 points last week.
With McLaurin out he is the one proven target left, and the short throws all go his way.
Washington ranks 31st against QBs, but his giveaways keep cutting drives short.
Indianapolis ranks 28th against backs, but Washington's run game is weak and Ekeler takes a share.

take.head: Cardinals edge it; Giants cover at home
take.lean:
Jacoby Brissett gets all day against a Giants pass rush that has almost nothing left. New York sacked the quarterback on just 1.0 percent of pass plays this season, and that was with Brian Burns. Burns is now out for the season with a torn ACL, so Brissett gets a clean pocket and an easy afternoon of reading the field.

Brissett gets the ball to Trey McBride and Michael Wilson. Wilson drew 34.0 percent of the targets last week. A Giants defense that ranks 28th against the pass has no answer for him on the outside. McBride works the middle on volume, the way he has all season. With James Conner on IR, Jeremiyah Love handled 77.8 percent of the carries last week and gets the early-down work against a Giants run defense that is ordinary.

Arizona's offense has one weakness, and it keeps this game close. The Cardinals almost never hit a big play. Their drives are long strings of short completions, and long drives stall. Arizona moves the ball between the 20s all day but settles for field goals too often to pull away.

The Giants want to run, and they hit the wrong defense for it. New York passes only 38.2 percent of the time when the game is close. Arizona's run defense is one of the league's stingiest. Cam Skattebo needed 20 carries to reach 60 yards against the Titans, and this front is tougher. Expect a lot of short runs.

That puts the game in Jameis Winston's hands, which sounds like bad news. He has been dreadful through 55 pass plays this season. But Arizona's pass defense ranks 30th and lost Will Johnson, a defensive back who played 89.5 percent of snaps before going on IR. Winston will throw into tight windows no matter who lines up across from him. Against this secondary, enough of those throws get completed. Malik Nabers took 28.6 percent of the targets last week and gets the soft coverage. Isaiah Likely faces a defense that ranks 28th against tight ends.

The market swung this game completely when Jaxson Dart went on IR, and that swing went far enough. Arizona's quarterback is better and should win, but a Cardinals team without big plays doesn't build a lead the Giants can't erase late. Arizona wins a game that's still in doubt in the fourth quarter. Brissett and Wilson are the best starts in it, and Nabers is the Giants player to trust.
take.vs: Agree Arizona wins, but by less. The Giants land near their 21 because Arizona's secondary leaks, and Arizona's lack of big plays keeps it short of 23.5.
take.risk: Winston keeps throwing it to the other team the way he has in 2026, and Brissett's clean pocket turns this into a two-score Arizona win.

ats.edge: Arizona's 30th-ranked pass defense, without Will Johnson, lets Winston and Nabers keep the Giants within a field goal.

take.vs_blind: Held near the blind Arizona by 1.5. The line's swing from the Giants by 7 reflects Dart going to IR, which the research already had. Total trimmed from 43.5 because Arizona rarely hits big plays.

notes.text: With Brian Burns out for the season (torn ACL), the Giants' thin pass rush gets even thinner. Brissett is a sneaky streaming QB.
Arizona stuffs the run but gets torched through the air: a tough spot for Skattebo, a better one for Nabers even with Winston throwing.

players.why: The Giants barely pressured passers even with Burns, and Burns is gone for the season.

take.head: Stroud, Lamb feast; Dallas keeps it close
take.lean:
Stroud gets Nico Collins back against a Dallas secondary that ranks 31st in the league at stopping the pass. That secondary gets almost no help up front: Dallas sacks the quarterback on just 2.1 percent of pass plays.

Houston needs this matchup, because little else on its offense works. Its run game is among the league's worst, and David Montgomery and Woody Marks split the carries. The line gives up sacks more often than the league average. In week 3, with Collins out, Stroud scored 11.7 points and the Texans put up 17 in a loss to the Colts.

Collins changes that. In week 1 he drew a 27.0 percent target share, and Stroud finally has a receiver the defense has to account for on every snap. Houston throws early and often instead of running Montgomery into the line. Dalton Schultz goes back to a secondary role after picking up extra targets while Collins was out.

Dallas answers the same way. Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb have been nearly perfect together, and Houston is missing linebackers Azeez Al-Shaair and Henry To'oTo'o, the two players who cover the middle of the field. The Texans already give up the 30th-most points to receivers. Without those linebackers, Lamb and Jake Ferguson find open space on routes across the middle.

Houston wins one matchup clearly: its pass rush sacks quarterbacks on 10.1 percent of pass plays. Dallas's line rarely gives up sacks, though, and Prescott gets the ball out on time. The rush gets home a few times without stopping the drives.

Javonte Williams takes the hit on the Dallas side. Houston gives up the fewest points to running backs in the league, and Dallas's own run game is below average. With an easy matchup through the air, the Cowboys put the game on Prescott, and Williams gets his touches without the big runs.

Expect a back-and-forth game through the air. Houston has the home crowd and gets back the receiver it has missed, so it edges the game late. Still, Dallas's passing game is the best unit on the field and keeps the game within a field goal. George Pickens gets his share of the targets behind Lamb, but he does not have a big game.
take.vs: Close to the market on Houston, but Dallas scores more than its implied 22.8: Houston's missing linebackers and a defense 30th against receivers let Prescott keep pace.
take.risk: Houston's pass rush sacks Prescott and stalls drives, or Houston's line gives up sacks again and Stroud never gets time to find Collins.

ats.edge: Houston plays without its top two linebackers and gives up the 30th-most WR points; Dak and Lamb keep this within a field goal.

take.vs_blind: The margin barely moved, from HOU by 1.5 to 2. The total rose from 47.5 because both pass defenses rank among the league's worst and Collins is confirmed back.

notes.text: Nico Collins practiced fully Friday and has no injury tag, so he is back from his hamstring injury for Dallas.
Dak to CeeDee Lamb: 20 catches on 25 targets, 309 yards and 3 TDs with no interceptions. Houston is without its top two linebackers.
Houston's run game is one of the league's worst. Stroud's passing is the better fantasy play against one of the league's worst pass defenses.

take.head: Packers edge it, Bucs cover behind Irving
take.lean:
Jalon Daniels is an undrafted rookie making his first start, and he gets a Green Bay defense that has given up 30.3 points a game. The debut is softer than the quarterback change suggests. Baker Mayfield's passing was already among the league's worst before he hurt his thumb, so Tampa isn't losing a passing game that worked. It is swapping one that stalled for one with a quarterback who can run.

Daniels' running matters most against Tampa's biggest flaw. Bucs passers have been sacked on 10.7% of pass plays, and a quarterback who runs turns some of those sacks into scrambles. His running also opens room for Bucky Irving. Green Bay allows the most fantasy points to running backs in the league, and Irving's carry share climbed to 71.4 last week. His sore glute let him practice Thursday, and he is the Bucs player to start with confidence. Kenny Gainwell stays an afterthought.

The Bucs' passing game shrinks to short throws. Emeka Egbuka leads Tampa's receivers in targets and Cade Otton plays nearly every snap, so they are the rookie's first reads. Chris Godwin Jr. missed Wednesday's practice with a sore ankle and drops to third in line.

Green Bay's offense has the opposite problem. The Packers run for 48.7 yards a game, Josh Jacobs is on the commissioner's exempt list, and the offensive line is missing starters, Jacob Monk among them. Tampa's run defense is among the league's best. MarShawn Lloyd has nowhere to go, and this becomes Jordan Love's game whether Green Bay wants it or not.

Love has the receivers to carry it. Christian Watson and Matthew Golden have both drawn heavy targets, and Tampa is without defensive back Benjamin Morrison and pass rusher Rueben Bain. Tampa still holds receivers down overall, so Love lands near his projection, not past it. Tucker Kraft finds the open space, against a defense that ranks 21st against tight ends.

That leaves a close game settled by Love's arm late. Tampa's fumbles keep the Packers in front: the Bucs have lost 4 of their 5. But with both defenses giving up points this easily, the scoring runs past what the market expects, and Tampa stays within a field goal.
take.vs: Agree on Green Bay winning, but Tampa scores more. The total fell after Mayfield's injury, yet his passing was already poor and Green Bay's defense allows 30.3 points a game.
take.risk: Daniels melts under the rush Tampa already allows, the fumbles keep coming, and Love's receivers beat a thin secondary for a two-score Packers win.

ats.edge: Mayfield was already passing at a bottom-tier level; the line moved to GB as if losing him were a big downgrade.

take.vs_blind: Held near the blind GB by 3, trimmed to 2 because Green Bay's line is missing starters against a run defense this stout; total eased from 40.5 to 40.

notes.text: Bucs QB Baker Mayfield (thumb) is out at least three weeks. Undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels, a running QB from Kansas, makes his first start.
Green Bay ranks last in rushing (48.7 yards a game) with Josh Jacobs on the commissioner's exempt list and a banged-up line. Fade Packers RBs.

take.head: Lawrence beats a thin Bengals secondary
take.lean:
Trevor Lawrence comes to Cincinnati playing the best football of his career, and he faces a Bengals secondary that is missing pieces. Kyle Dugger is out, Bryan Cook is questionable with an ankle and Jalen Davis is on IR. That leaves the back end short on bodies against a passer who is getting far more out of each throw than he did in 2025.

Cincinnati's defense looks better on paper this year. It ranks 8th against the pass, but it built that rank with its safeties healthy, and the same unit gave up 28.9 points a game last season. Quarterbacks already score well against it: it ranks 22nd in points allowed to the position. With the depth thin behind the cornerbacks, Lawrence gets clean throws over the middle.

Jacksonville doesn't settle for field goals. The Jaguars have turned 88.9% of their red-zone trips into touchdowns, so their drives end in the end zone. Bhayshul Tuten benefits most. He handles half the carries and has beaten his projection every week. Parker Washington leads the targets and keeps getting open against the backup safeties. Brenton Strange has gone quiet, but Cincinnati gives tight ends the 24th-most points, so this is his week to turn targets into catches.

The Bengals have the harder job. Jacksonville's defense allows 12.0 points a game, and quarterbacks score less against it than against all but two teams. Joe Burrow keeps the passing game moving, but in this matchup his production runs through one man. Ja'Marr Chase drew 32.4% of the targets last week and gets that volume again. The Bengals have nobody else they can count on.

The running game won't take any pressure off Burrow. Cincinnati's runs lose ground on most plays, and Jacksonville ranks 6th against backs. Chase Brown has fallen short of his projection two weeks running, and that continues. Mike Gesicki goes up against a defense that ranks 7th against tight ends.

The game comes down to touchdowns against field goals. The Bengals have scored touchdowns on only half of their red-zone trips. Jacksonville's defense has allowed touchdowns on 20.0% of opponents' trips. The Jaguars score touchdowns on their drives and Cincinnati settles for field goals on too many of theirs. That gap holds all afternoon, and Jacksonville leaves with the win.
take.vs: Disagree. The market gives CIN 27, but JAX's defense allows 12.0 a game and ranks 3rd against QBs. JAX tops its 24.5 against a thinned Bengals secondary.
take.risk: Burrow and Chase hit big plays on a JAX defense that allows WRs 25.9 a game, and Cincinnati scores touchdowns instead of field goals.

ats.edge: CIN is without Dugger and Davis, and maybe Cook, against Lawrence's best start; JAX's defense allows 12.0 points a game.

take.vs_blind: Margin held at JAX by 3. The market is backing home field and Burrow, and no fact here changes the secondary read. Total moved up from 46.5 because both passing games are strong.

notes.text: With rookie WR Colbie Young out, Dohnte Meyers stays the Bengals' No. 3 receiver behind Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins this week.

take.head: Rams cover as Eagles run out of receivers
take.lean:
Stafford will have time to throw against an Eagles defense that hasn't taken the ball away once in 3 games. Philadelphia sacks the quarterback on 3.1% of pass plays, about half the league rate. Now it also plays without Baun, the linebacker who was on the field for nearly every snap. That leaves a soft middle and a pass rush that doesn't get home, which suits a Rams offense that passes more than most when the game is close.

The Rams win this game on throws. Philadelphia's pass defense ranks 23rd, and its defense ranks 25th against receivers. Adams has carried the passing game with 15 catches for 332 yards the last two weeks. Nacua returns from 2 missed games, and the Rams will ease him back. That keeps Adams as the first read for another week, and he beats his projection. Stafford threw for 390 yards last week. Against this rush he moves the ball all afternoon.

Los Angeles stalls near the goal line. The Rams have scored touchdowns on just 45.5% of their red-zone trips, and those stalled drives turn into field goals. That keeps the game close enough to stay interesting. Kyren Williams is the goal-line back after taking 65.2% of the carries last week. Philadelphia ranks 10th against backs, so he lands near his number and doesn't blow past it.

Philadelphia can't match the Rams through the air. Its passing game was below average even with Smith and Goedert, and the offense scored 18.3 points a game. Both are out. That leaves Wicks, Lemon and the recently signed Moore at receiver, with Ertz at tight end, against a pass defense that ranks 7th. The Rams' rush is thin too, with Garrett on injured reserve and Donald out. Hurts gets time, but he has nobody to throw to. His runs keep him a usable starter, but he doesn't get above a mid-range finish.

Wicks is the one Eagles pass catcher to start. He has drawn 20% of the targets with Smith in the lineup. Without Smith he's the first read on every pass play, and against the Rams' 13th-ranked defense against receivers he clears a low projection. Barkley goes the other way. The Rams rank 7th against backs, and a Philadelphia team that trails all game hands him fewer carries than his 10.8 projection needs.

On the Rams' side, Higbee has the worst draw: Philadelphia ranks 2nd against tight ends. Ertz has a similar problem across the field against a Rams defense that ranks 5th against the position. The Rams build a lead with Stafford's arm and keep it with field goals. Philadelphia's offense doesn't have the pieces to get back into it.
take.vs: Agree with LA's 23. PHI lands a shade under its 19.5 because its passing game is down to Wicks, Lemon and Ertz against a pass defense that ranks 7th.
take.risk: Hurts runs in two scores, or the Rams' 6 giveaways in 3 games keep coming and hand Philadelphia short fields.

ats.edge: PHI lost its top WR and TE from an offense that already scored only 18.3 a game, and LA gets Nacua back

take.vs_blind: Held near my blind LA by 4.5. I shaded the total under 42.5 because LA scores touchdowns on only 45.5% of red-zone trips.

take.head: Bills cover, Patriots stall in the red zone
take.lean:
Drake Maye drops back behind a patched-up line. Greg Van Roten is on IR, Mike Onwenu is hurt and Morgan Moses is questionable. Buffalo's front reaches the quarterback more often than most, and Maye has no A.J. Brown to throw to quickly with Brown on IR. Maye scored 3.8 last week, and this line gives him no more time than the one that produced that.

The pressure feeds New England's real problem: it can't finish drives. The Patriots score 12 a game and have reached the end zone on just 1 of 7 red-zone trips. Maye was far better in 2025, and Buffalo has given up 26 a game, so New England moves the ball through the middle of the field. Then it stalls close to the goal line and kicks field goals.

Buffalo's offense has a tougher test than its scoring suggests. New England's defense ranks 4th against the pass and allows the fewest points to tight ends. That is bad news for Dalton Kincaid. But Christian Gonzalez is out, and that changes where Josh Allen throws. DJ Moore drew 38.5 percent of the targets last week, and now he works the outside against the Patriots' backup corners.

Christian Barmore is out too, which opens the middle for James Cook. He took 72.7 percent of the carries last week, and a Buffalo lead keeps feeding him. Allen lands close to his projection. The Patriots allow the fifth-fewest points to quarterbacks, and Cook handles the short scores Allen usually runs in himself.

Once Buffalo leads by more than a score, New England has to throw, and Mack Hollins gets the volume. He drew 30.0 percent of the targets last week. Buffalo ranks 29th against receivers, and its corner Christian Benford is questionable. The Patriots' backfield goes the other way. Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson split the carries, and falling behind takes the run game away from both.

Buffalo wins clearly, but not in a shootout. New England's pass defense holds the Bills below their usual scoring, and the Patriots' red-zone failures cap their side. That keeps the combined score well short of what the market expects.
take.vs: Lower on both sides. NE's 12 a game says it does not reach 21, and NE's defense, 4th against the pass and allowing 17 a game, keeps Buffalo under its implied total.
take.risk: Maye finds his 2025 form against a Buffalo defense allowing 26 a game, or Allen's giveaways hand NE a short field and the red-zone touchdowns it hasn't scored.

ats.edge: NE scores 12 a game with 1 TD on 7 red-zone trips, and its line is without Van Roten and Onwenu against Buffalo's rush.

take.vs_blind: The margin held near the blind BUF by 8.5, and the line's move from BUF by 5.5 to 7 agrees. The total came down from 45.5 because NE's defense allows only 17 a game.

He splits carries with Henderson, and falling behind cuts the run game.

take.head: Jets stay inside the hook at Soldier Field
take.lean:
Tyson Bagent takes over a Bears offense that was rolling, and he faces the one thing the Jets do well: stop the run. New York's run defense ranks among the league's best this season, so a backup quarterback won't get the easy early downs he needs. Bagent's 9 pass plays this year went badly. Case Keenum ran this offense well in last week's 27-7 win over the Eagles, but Bagent gets the start, and left tackle Braxton Jones is out in front of him.

That puts D'Andre Swift in a tough spot. He has scored about 10 points in each of the last two weeks while getting more than half the carries, and the Jets' front won't give him more room than that. His floor comes from catching passes, and Bagent will check down to him often. Kyle Monangai's share of the work keeps shrinking, and running into this defense won't turn that around.

So Chicago has to throw, and Luther Burden III is the target. His target share has gone up every week, to 32.4 percent against Philadelphia, and the Jets' pass defense sits 17th, right in the middle of the league. Kalif Raymond's big week came on a near-perfect line from Keenum, and that efficiency won't come with him. Rome Odunze keeps playing nearly every snap and doing little with it. Colston Loveland faces a defense that allows the third-fewest points to tight ends, which isn't where his slow start ends.

The Jets come into this even thinner. Geno Smith has passed well this season after a rough 2025 in Las Vegas, but Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell, Mason Taylor and left guard Dylan Parham are all out. A run game that was already among the league's worst loses its best back. That makes the Jets a pass-only team against a Chicago pass defense that ranks 5th, and Smith will spend the afternoon under pressure.

What's left is Garrett Wilson. With Mitchell and Taylor out, nobody else on this roster can command targets, and Wilson already drew 36.1 percent of them last week. Isaiah Williams and Josh Reynolds are filling in. Kenyon Sadiq is questionable with a back injury against a defense that holds tight ends down. Wilson will get double-digit targets because there's no one else to throw to.

Braelon Allen and Isaiah Davis split Hall's backfield work. Davis hasn't played a snap all year, so Allen gets most of the carries. The yards per carry won't be good, but the volume carries him past a low projection.

This turns into a slow, field-position game. Neither offense can do the thing it wants to do most, and the Jets have given the ball away once in three games, so they don't hand Chicago short fields. The Bears' defense and home crowd are enough to win. They aren't enough to pull away from a team that protects the ball, and a three-point game leaves the hook with New York.
take.vs: Close to the market's 23.5 to 20, a bit lower on both sides: each offense lost a key piece and runs into the other defense's strength, Jets run D and Bears pass D.
take.risk: Bagent plays the way Keenum did in week 3, Burden and Raymond keep producing, and Chicago pulls away late from a Jets team with one healthy receiver.

ats.edge: Bagent's 9 pass plays this year went badly; a field-goal Bears win is the likeliest result, and the hook sits on the Jets' side.

take.head: Ravens roll, but Titans sneak inside the number
take.lean:
Lamar Jackson gets to throw against a Titans defense that holds up against the run but gives way through the air. Tennessee ranks 21st in how many points opposing pass plays add, and Jackson has been one of the league's best passers this season.

Baltimore doesn't throw much, though. The Ravens pass less than almost any team when the game is close, and once they lead they hand it to Derrick Henry, who has taken the bulk of the carries every week. Last week he carried 26 times and scored twice against Dallas. Tennessee ranks 19th against backs. With a big lead and four quarters of handoffs, Henry beats his projection.

That same pattern explains a number that looks wrong at first: Tennessee has allowed the 2nd fewest fantasy points to quarterbacks. Teams build a lead on the Titans and then stop throwing. Jackson will be efficient but won't throw often, and his legs carry his line to about where it is projected. Zay Flowers is listed questionable with a hamstring, but he practiced in full Thursday and remains the target leader when he plays. Mark Andrews is the Raven to fade. Tennessee ranks 4th against tight ends, and Andrews already gets the fewest snaps of Baltimore's main targets.

Tennessee's offense gives Baltimore plenty of room. The Titans score 12.3 points a game on very few plays, and they just lost 12-7 to the Giants. Coach Robert Saleh is still telling Cam Ward to be smarter with the football, and when Ward is chasing a game late he falls back into forcing throws. The Ravens will be well ahead by halftime.

The cover is in the second half. Baltimore's defense has given up 26.0 points a game, Dallas scored 31 on it last week, and Trey Hendrickson is out after finger surgery, so the Ravens lose their best pass rusher. Once the Ravens lead comfortably and settle into running Henry, Ward will have time to throw. Wan'Dale Robinson is the receiver he trusts: he drew 31.4 percent of the targets last week, and Baltimore ranks 21st against receivers. Robinson beats his projection on catches that come after the game is decided.

Tony Pollard loses out the most from that script. Tyjae Spears is expected back from his ankle injury and will split the work, and a team that is behind stops running. Tennessee's late touchdown doesn't change who wins, but it is the one that decides the spread.
take.vs: Agree that BAL scores 27. TEN lands just above its 15.5 because a Ravens defense without Hendrickson has allowed 26.0 a game and gives up points late.
take.risk: Ward turns it over early, or Flowers plays at full speed, and BAL leads by 20 before TEN's late possessions.

ats.edge: BAL's defense allows 26.0 points a game and lost Hendrickson; TEN adds late points against it to stay inside the number

take.head: Vikings win, but Miami stays inside 10
take.lean:
Aaron Jones gets the ball against a Miami defense that gives up 27.1 points a game to running backs, 30th in the league. Kyler Murray also gets a clean pocket, because the Dolphins have no sacks in 3 games. Minnesota's passing game doesn't need to be good this week. It just needs to avoid mistakes while Jones carries the load.

That matters because Minnesota's offense is not good. Justin Jefferson is out with an ankle injury, so the passing game runs through Jordan Addison. Addison drew 36.0 percent of the targets last week and scored on a 41-yard catch, while Murray went 15-for-39 in that game. Against the league's worst pass defense, Addison gets his catches. But this offense rarely makes big plays, and an offense that moves in short gains is slow to pull away.

Miami's day ends on the other side of the ball. Minnesota allows 13.7 points a game and has given up 1 touchdown in 9 trips inside its 20. Miami scores 12.0 a game and has lost De'Von Achane for the season with a torn knee ligament. Ollie Gordon II carried 17 times for 41 yards and a touchdown last week, and Jaylen Wright is healthy again to share the work. Gordon's carries clear his low projection, but a defense that ranks 4th against backs leaves no room for a long run.

Malik Willis has to throw against a pass defense that ranks 2nd. His legs keep a few drives alive, but they don't produce points. Malik Washington gets steady targets for short gains. Tyreek Hill comes in with no recent games and lines up against the toughest part of this defense.

Minnesota leads at halftime on Jones's carries and a couple of Addison catches, then plays it safe. That same caution keeps Miami close. A Vikings team that throws only when it has to doesn't add the late touchdown that turns 9 points into 14, and Miami picks up a late field goal against a soft, protect-the-lead defense. With two offenses this weak, the scoreboard stays quiet.
take.vs: Miami lands near its 14.2. Minnesota falls just short of 24.2, because an offense this short on big plays rarely runs up a double-digit margin.
take.risk: Murray hits Addison deep twice against a secondary with no pass rush, and Minnesota pulls away past 10 early.

ats.edge: Minnesota rarely makes big plays and Murray has struggled throwing; a team built like that wins by 9, not by double digits.

take.head: McCaffrey runs SF past Denver
take.lean:
Christian McCaffrey gets a Denver run defense that has fallen apart. A year ago this unit allowed 18.3 points a game and was one of the league's best. This season it still holds up against the pass, ranking 9th, but running backs have hit it hard, and it ranks 29th against them. McCaffrey is getting the work to take advantage. Last week he played 83% of the snaps and took 65.2% of the carries, and Kaelon Black faded into the background.

The run game also protects San Francisco's passing game where it is weakest this week. Brock Purdy has been the best passer in the league over three games, with four touchdowns on 27 throws last week. Mike Evans is fighting a rib injury, though. He played only 33% of the snaps last week, and Demarcus Robinson is on injured reserve. That leaves few outside threats against a Denver defense that hits the quarterback more often than almost anyone. Kyle Shanahan doesn't need to test that. He hands it to McCaffrey and sends the short throws to George Kittle, who drew 26.9% of the targets last week and faces a Denver defense that ranks 19th against tight ends. Purdy stays efficient on fewer attempts and lands near his projection instead of reaching 30 again.

Denver can't match that on offense. Bo Nix completed 17 of 34 passes in last week's win over the Rams. The Broncos have scored 10 first-half points in three games, last in the league, and they throw far more than most teams when the game is close. San Francisco's defense without Nick Bosa puts less heat on the passer. It still ranks 8th against quarterbacks and 8th against receivers, and it almost never gives up the deep shot Denver needs to make up for missed throws. Jaylen Waddle is the only Bronco receiver who can break a game open. Courtland Sutton and Evan Engram keep getting targets and producing little.

Denver falls behind early, and that splits its backfield. J.K. Dobbins took 68% of the carries last week but catches almost nothing, so his value disappears once the Broncos have to throw. RJ Harvey takes those snaps and turns short catches into garbage-time points that keep the final score respectable.

The line moved toward Denver on the Bosa and Evans news. Neither one changes the matchup that decides this game. Both offenses run few plays: San Francisco averages 53.3 a game against a league norm of 60.6. A slow, run-heavy 49ers lead that Nix can't chase down doesn't reach the shootout the total now expects.
take.vs: Agree that SF scores near 26. Denver lands below 22.8: it has 10 first-half points in three games and SF rarely allows big plays.
take.risk: Evans plays a full game and Purdy keeps throwing touchdowns, or Nix repeats last week's 24.1 points and this turns into a shootout over the total.

ats.edge: The line slid on the Bosa and Evans news, but Denver ranks 29th against backs, and that is where SF wins this game.

take.head: Chiefs beat the Raiders through Kelce
take.lean:
Kirk Cousins has made the Raiders a passing team that works. On Sunday he throws into the Chiefs defense that gives up the fewest fantasy points of any team to quarterbacks, and also to wide receivers. Las Vegas has nothing to fall back on. Its run game is one of the league's worst, so when the outside throws dry up, the Raiders can't move the ball on the ground either.

That puts everything on Brock Bowers. He drew 13 targets in his Week 3 return, and Kansas City ranks only in the middle of the league against tight ends. Cousins goes to Bowers when Tre Tucker and Jalen Nailor are covered, and against this secondary they will be covered most of the day. Ashton Jeanty keeps his snaps but won't gain many yards. Runs into this front go nowhere, and Bowers takes the short throws that usually rescue a back's day.

On paper the Raiders defense looks like the better unit. It ranks first in the league against the pass, and its rush gets a sack on 8.8 percent of pass plays. On Sunday that rush faces Kahlil Benson, an undrafted rookie starting at left tackle for the injured Josh Simmons. That is the one real threat to Patrick Mahomes. But this defense has also forced 12 fumbles in three games, and no defense keeps knocking the ball loose that often. Kansas City has turned it over twice all year. Fewer free possessions take away the edge that has kept Las Vegas in games.

Mahomes goes after the soft spot, not the strength. Las Vegas ranks 30th against tight ends, and Travis Kelce is the answer to a fast rush: a quick, short throw over the middle before the pressure gets home. Rashee Rice faces a secondary that ranks 4th against wideouts, and that is where the Raiders win their snaps. Kenneth Walker III gets the rest of the work. The Raiders stop the run well, but Walker's catches keep him near his usual output.

Late in the game the difference between these offenses shows. Kansas City can hand the ball to Walker to protect a lead. Las Vegas, down a score, has no run game to lean on and has to keep throwing into the league's best coverage against receivers. Cousins has been sharp this season, but this is his hardest test, and the Chiefs pull away just enough.
take.vs: Agree on KC's 26. LV lands short of its implied 21.5: no run game, and it has to throw into the defense that ranks 1st against both QBs and WRs.
take.risk: LV's rush beats Benson, the fumbles keep coming, and a heavy target load for Bowers turns a one-score game toward the home team.

ats.edge: LV's defense rests on 12 forced fumbles in three games; that pace fades, and LV can't run the ball to keep Mahomes off the field

take.vs_blind: Held KC as the winner and moved from a 4.5-point margin to 6. LV's run game can't threaten KC, and its forced-fumble pace won't last. The market had the same 4.5 as my research.

take.head: Seattle smothers Herbert again, JSN feasts
take.lean:
Justin Herbert drops back into the one defense built to make his season worse. The Chargers are 0-3, Jim Harbaugh has publicly told him to 'be better', and he is starting without his left tackle against a Seattle front that gets to the passer often. Herbert has a career-low 59.1% completion rate and an interception in every start. His protection was already leaking before the tackle went down.

In a normal week the fix is to run the ball and shorten the field. That doesn't work here. Seattle's run defense is the best part of the league's stingiest unit, and it allows the 5th-fewest fantasy points to backs. Omarion Hampton's snaps fell to 42 percent last week, with Kimani Vidal taking a bigger share. A shared backfield running into that wall gives Herbert no help, and the Chargers end up throwing on obvious passing downs.

Those passes don't go anywhere. Seattle allows almost no big plays, so Los Angeles has to drive the length of the field in short gains, and the hits and turnovers kill those drives. Ladd McConkey sat out Thursday's practice with the foot injury, so even if he plays he's working at less than full speed. Tre Harris has earned the steady short targets, with a 21.2 percent share last week, and he becomes the outlet in a game where Herbert has no time. Quentin Johnston keeps getting volume and keeps doing nothing with it.

The other side is the reverse. Sam Darnold came back last week and threw for 379 yards and 4 TDs. Now he faces a Chargers secondary where Derwin James, Elijah Molden and Donte Jackson are all questionable, and a defense allowing 25.3 points a game. Jaxon Smith-Njigba has drawn at least 31.1 percent of the targets every week and topped 22 fantasy points in each game. Against a thinned-out secondary he's the safest big score on the slate.

Seattle's own running game keeps this from becoming a blowout. Jadarian Price is out and Charbonnet isn't eligible yet, which leaves Emanuel Wilson as the lead back. Last week Wilson turned nine carries into 14 yards. He gets the carries and a short touchdown chance, and not much else. Seattle also has two lost fumbles already this season. Expect drives that stall in the red zone and some field goals.

That sets the game script: Seattle builds a lead through the air with Smith-Njigba, and the Chargers chase it by passing into the rush. The Seahawks pull away without the score going high, and the 17.8 points the market expects from Los Angeles assumes an offense that hasn't shown up in three weeks.

take.risk: Seattle's fumbles hand LAC short fields, or a healthy McConkey gives Herbert quick throws that beat the rush.

take.head: Lions pick on a Panthers secondary without Horn
take.lean:
Amon-Ra St. Brown gets a Carolina secondary playing without Jaycee Horn, and that decides this game. Before going on IR, Horn played 87.3 percent of the snaps. A rookie and a backup now start outside. Carolina's defense ranks 2nd against wide receivers, but Horn was on the field for every game that built that rank. Against Jared Goff, who has been one of the league's best passers this season, it will not hold up.

Detroit's offense runs through two players, and both have easy matchups. St. Brown wins underneath on the new corners all night. Jahmyr Gibbs faces a defense that ranks 31st against running backs. Gibbs doesn't need the Lions' weak run blocking, because he does his damage as a receiver too: he drew 25.8 percent of the targets last week. Near the goal line Detroit scores touchdowns instead of field goals, and Carolina's defense has allowed touchdowns on 85.7 percent of opponents' red-zone trips. Those touchdowns go to Gibbs and St. Brown, which keeps Goff close to his projection instead of well past it.

Carolina keeps pace through the air, because the ground gives it nothing. The Panthers' run game is among the league's worst. Chuba Hubbard's value is all volume, and he had 82.6 percent of the carries last week. Bryce Young is a much better passer than he was last season, and he faces the league's worst defense against quarterbacks. Detroit has allowed 31.7 points a game, and starting cornerback D.J. Reed is questionable with a rib injury.

The problem is who catches the ball. Xavier Legette is on IR, and Jalen Coker was limited in practice with a quad injury, so he is unlikely to be at full speed if he plays. That leaves Tetairoa McMillan as the clear top target. He drew 31.2 percent of the targets in week 2, and this week that share comes back. Darren Waller faces the defense that ranks last against tight ends, and Young throws to him over the middle all night.

Carolina can't win a shootout because of its line. Left guard Damien Lewis is out, and Detroit's pass rush brings Young down on 8.3 percent of his pass plays. Two or three of those sacks stall Carolina drives in Detroit territory and turn them into field goals. Detroit keeps scoring touchdowns. Jameson Williams is the Lion left out: Gibbs, St. Brown and Sam LaPorta take the volume, and Williams has finished under his projection every week.

take.risk: Coker plays fully, Carolina's rush keeps St. Brown quiet, and Detroit's red-zone trips end in field goals instead of touchdowns.

ats.edge: Carolina's 2nd-ranked defense against receivers was built with Horn, now on IR; a rookie and a backup start against St. Brown.

take.head: Bijan runs Atlanta past a thinned Saints front
take.lean:
Bijan Robinson faces a Saints front missing linebacker Kaden Elliss and edge rusher Carl Granderson, and Pete Werner is questionable. New Orleans already ranks 29th against running backs with those players on the field. Robinson comes in off a 194-yard rushing night against Green Bay. Atlanta does not need anything clever here: hand him the ball and keep handing it to him.

Atlanta's ugly early-season passing came with Cooper Rush and Jack Strand under center. Michael Penix came back last week, and the offense put 35 points on the Packers. Atlanta passes far less than the league does when the game is close. Penix doesn't have to carry this team; he has to make the Saints pay for crowding the line. Drake London drew 43.5 percent of the targets in Penix's return, so whatever passing there is runs through him. Penix lands near his projection because the volume goes to the backs. London is the one who turns those throws into points.

New Orleans has to answer through the air because it has nothing on the ground. With Travis Etienne on IR, Alvin Kamara takes the lead role against the defense that allows the fewest points to backs. He has scored under 5 points in both of his games. That leaves Tyler Shough, who has beaten his projection in all three games, throwing to Chris Olave, who gets close to a third of the team's targets. Atlanta has A.J. Terrell on IR and ranks 26th against receivers, so Olave wins his matchup. Juwan Johnson gets his usual work against a defense that ranks 24th against tight ends.

The Saints run more plays than almost anyone, so this one stays high-scoring. Both offenses will move the ball. The difference is how each one does it. New Orleans puts everything on Shough's arm, and the Saints have already given the ball away 7 times in three games. Atlanta can lean on its best player against a defense missing its middle linebacker and an edge rusher, and those runs only get easier late in the game.

Kyle Pitts gets lost in all of this. He hasn't scored more than 2 points in any game, and Robinson and London take every touch that matters.

take.risk: Penix's return is one game. If ATL's passing slips back and Shough hits Olave deep early, NO's fast tempo turns this into a Saints shootout win.

ats.edge: ATL's weak season passing came with Rush and Strand. Penix is back, and NO is without Elliss and Granderson against Bijan.
